client: I just don't know how to get through my days since my grandma passed away. Everything feels heavy, and I keep spacing out at work - like I'll just stare at my computer screen for twenty minutes without realizing it. Part of me thinks talking about it won't help because nothing will bring her back.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot of grief, and it's understandable that concentrating feels difficult right now. When you mention that talking about it might not help, is there something specific you're worried might happen if you open up about your feelings?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I guess I'm afraid if I start talking about it, I'll just fall apart completely. Like the sadness will swallow me whole. Plus, people keep telling me "she's in a better place" and that just makes me angry - like they're dismissing how much this hurts.
therapist: It sounds like you're holding onto a lot of pain, and there's a fear that letting it out might feel overwhelming. When people say things like "she's in a better place," it seems to add to your frustration rather than help - would you like to share what kind of support would feel more meaningful to you right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't even know what would help - maybe just someone listening without trying to fix it? The worst part is I keep expecting to see her when I go home, or I'll reach for my phone to call her before remembering. It's like my brain hasn't caught up that she's gone.
therapist: Those moments when you instinctively reach for your phone or expect to see her must feel so jarring - like losing her all over again each time. You mentioned wanting someone to just listen, which makes me wonder if part of what hurts is feeling like your grief isn't fully being acknowledged as it is?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah... exactly. It's like people want me to "move on" already, but I'm not ready. And when they don't acknowledge how bad it still hurts, it makes me feel even more alone. Like my grief is some inconvenient thing they have to tiptoe around.
therapist: There's a real pain in feeling rushed through your grief, especially when what you need most is the space to honor what you're feeling. That sense of loneliness when others seem uncomfortable with your pain—would you say it adds another layer of hurt to what you're already carrying?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It absolutely does. Like not only am I grieving, but now I'm also grieving alone because no one wants to sit with me in this pain. And then I start feeling guilty for being "too much" - like I should be over it by now, but I'm just not.
therapist: It sounds like there's a lot of weight in feeling like your grief is "too much"—almost as if you're carrying it alone while also carrying this added burden of guilt. When you say you're not ready to "be over it," what would it feel like to give yourself permission to grieve at your own pace, without judgment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I don't even know how to do that - give myself permission, I mean. It's like there's this voice in my head saying I should be stronger or that I'm being selfish for still being so upset. I just wish I could turn that voice off, but it's always there, judging me.
therapist: It sounds like that inner voice is adding an extra layer of struggle on top of your grief, almost as if you're battling yourself while already carrying so much. What do you think it would feel like to imagine speaking to yourself with the same kindness you'd offer a close friend going through this loss?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: That's... hard to imagine. When my best friend lost her grandpa, I told her to take all the time she needed. But with myself? It feels different. Like I don't deserve that same patience, even though logically I know that's not true. It's just easier to be kind to others than to myself.
therapist: It sounds like you have so much compassion for others, but when it comes to yourself, that kindness feels harder to access. What do you think makes it so different to extend that same patience and understanding to yourself, even though you know it's what you deserve?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it's because I've always been taught to be strong and keep going, no matter what. With others, I can see their pain clearly, but with myself, it's like I'm supposed to push through it. Letting myself grieve feels like admitting weakness, even though I know that's not true. It's just... ingrained, I guess.
therapist: It sounds like there's a deep-rooted belief about needing to be strong that's making it hard to give yourself permission to grieve. What do you think it would feel like to challenge that belief, even just a little, by acknowledging that taking the time to grieve might actually be a form of strength, not weakness?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That feels really foreign to me - thinking of grief as strength. But maybe... maybe it takes more strength to face this pain than to push it away. It's just scary because if I admit how much this hurts, I'm afraid I'll never stop crying. Like the floodgates will open and I won't be able to close them.
therapist: It sounds like there's a real fear that if you let yourself fully feel the grief, it might overwhelm you. But perhaps those tears you're afraid of might also be a way of honoring your love for your grandma—a way of letting yourself feel what you've lost, rather than pushing it away. How does that idea sit with you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That idea... it makes sense, but it's also terrifying. I think part of me feels like if I let myself cry, I'll be proving everyone right - that I'm too emotional, too weak. And then I'll just disappoint people even more than I already have by not "getting over it" fast enough.
therapist: It sounds like there's a lot of fear about how others might perceive you if you allow yourself to fully grieve—like you're carrying not just the weight of your loss, but also the weight of others' expectations. What would it feel like to focus less on what others might think and more on what you need during this time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
